Louis Daguerre. A French painter and inventor who pioneered the daguerreotype, the first commercially viable photographic process, in 1839. His silvered copper plates produced sharp, detailed images that captivated the public and launched the age of practical photography, though each plate was a unique original rather than a reproducible negative.

Daguerre developed the daguerreotype process by exposing a silvered copper plate to light and developing it with mercury vapour to reveal a detailed photographic image. The French government purchased his patent in 1839 and released it to the world as a gift to humanity, accelerating global adoption of photography. He produced Boulevard du Temple, often cited as the first photograph to contain a human being—though the exposure was so long, between ten and fifteen minutes, that moving subjects vanished from the image.

Each daguerreotype was a single, unreproducible positive image. With no negatives, every plate was an original artwork, which boosted its appeal to wealthy collectors. His earlier career as a diorama painter, creating theatrical illusionists showing scenes through painted backlit panels, influenced his vision of capturing visual reality. Daguerreotypes dominated portraiture in the eighteen forties and fifties before being eclipsed by cheaper wet-collodion and albumen print processes.

Daguerre's work was built on his business partnership with Nicéphore Niépce, whose heliography was the conceptual foundation for the daguerreotype. He competed with William Henry Fox Talbot, the English rival who invented the calotype—a different early photography method. Eadweard Muybridge later used photography to study motion and anatomy. Alfred Stieglitz, working in the late nineteenth century, elevated photography to fine art, moving beyond the mere documentation that Daguerre had enabled.
